patient_actor_hidden.History: The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

Symptoms.Primary_Symptom: Sudden-onset sensation of the room spinning

patient_actor_hidden.Past_Medical_History: The patient is otherwise healthy with only a history of eczema. No prior episodes of similar nature.
patient_actor_hidden.Review_of_Systems: Denies headaches, hearing loss, tinnitus, loss of consciousness or neurological deficits.

objective_for_doctor: Assess and diagnose the patient presenting with sudden-onset symptoms of vertigo.

turns.content: Doctor: Let’s start—when did your sudden vertigo begin, and is it spinning (true vertigo) or more lightheadedness? Doctor: Also, do you have nausea/vomiting, new hearing loss or ringing in one ear, or headache?

Patient: It started just as I was going to bed, and it felt like the room was actually spinning for about 3 minutes. During that time I had nausea and vomited a few times, but I don’t have hearing loss, ringing in my ears, or a headache.

Doctor: Did the vertigo come in brief episodes (seconds to minutes) or was it continuous for hours/days, and does turning your head worsen it? Doctor: Do you feel unable to walk straight or have any numbness/weakness, trouble speaking, or double vision? REQUEST TEST: Bedside_neurologic_exam (finger-to-nose, gait, nystagmus, test of skew)

RESULTS: Vital signs stable (T 97.7°F/36.5°C, BP 134/85 mmHg, HR 85 bpm, RR 13/min, SpO2 98% on room air). Bedside neurologic findings: Healthy man with normal gait. Nystagmus present (physiologic), with severe symptoms and notable nystagmus when head is turned to the left and laid back; cranial nerve exam unremarkable. No information provided for finger-to-nose or test of skew, and no numbness/weakness, speech difficulty, or double vision reported in available data. Dix-Hallpike is positive, reproducing vertigo and nystagmus with left head turn and laid back position.

Doctor: The vertigo was brief but intense with clear room-spinning, nausea/vomiting, and a **positive Dix-Hallpike** reproducing symptoms with **directional nystagmus** when you turn your head left and lay back—this pattern strongly fits a peripheral positional cause. I’m going to diagnose this as **benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), likely left posterior canal**. DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), left posterior canal.
